headline: The more carbohydrate per kg you eat in the 1–2 days before a race, the more glycogen your muscles store
question: How much carbohydrate, for how long, and with what exercise beforehand, fills muscle glycogen stores the most before an endurance race?
design: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies that recorded carbohydrate intake and exercise for at least 24 h before a muscle biopsy. The descriptive part pooled 63 trials (42 randomised, 21 not) with 641 healthy adults. People aged 18–60 were eligible, but 83% of experiments were in 18–30-year-olds and no group's mean age was over 37. Most were endurance-trained or well-trained; the rest ranged from sedentary to elite team-sport players. Only 74 were women (12%), and 79% of trials studied men only. The meta-analysis kept 18 randomised trials with low risk of bias (13 crossover, 5 parallel-group) that compared a low-moderate intake (under 6.5 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹) against a high-very high intake (over 6.5 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹). Glycogen was measured from biopsies, in mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass.
findings:
Going from under to over 6.5 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ raised muscle glycogen by 191.9 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass (95% CI 142.8 to 241.1) in the crossover trials, and by 107.6 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass (95% CI −10.5 to 225.7, not significant) in the parallel-group trials. Heterogeneity was very high (I² = 94% and 92%).

Across all 63 trials, carbohydrate intake per kg explained about a third of the spread in glycogen between study groups in recreationally active people (r² = 0.332) and about half in endurance-trained people (r² = 0.490); in well-trained people alone the linear relation was not significant. The relation looked linear, with no clear plateau, though only five study groups ate around 12 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹. Where women and men ate the same carbohydrate per kg, they stored the same.

The authors suggest over 8 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h before a race, or 24–36 h after glycogen-depleting exercise with high glycaemic index carbohydrate.
limits: Heterogeneity was very high, and the subgroups (how much more carbohydrate, how many days) did not explain it, so the exact dose and duration stay uncertain; the authors say so themselves. Subgroup analyses are observational, and apart from heterogeneity the review did not rate imprecision, indirectness or publication bias (no GRADE). Many of the 63 trials were small, a third were not randomised, and only eight used any blinding. Only 74 of 641 participants were women, too few for a sex subgroup analysis, and the effect of menstrual cycle phase is unclear. In 65% of studies people rested while loading, unlike athletes who taper but still train. Glycogen, not race performance, was the outcome. No funding and no conflicts of interest were declared. The practical advice (over 8 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h) is a little firmer than the heterogeneous data behind it.
meaning: The lesson on carbohydrate stores (cell-molecules) gives muscle glycogen as about 400 g, "more after carbohydrate loading"; the lessons on glycolysis (bio-glycolysis) and the crossover (bio-crossover) teach that this limited store is what hard, long races run down. This review shows the main lever for filling it is simply how much carbohydrate per kg you eat in the last 1–2 days (it reports concentrations, not grams, so it doesn't test the 400 g figure itself). The fueling module (t4-fueling) will use it for how loading works in practice. It also shows a point from Evidence 101 (ev-pyramid): a large, significant pooled effect can still come with so much heterogeneity that the best dose is unknown.

variants.stem: According to the 2026 meta-analysis of carbohydrate loading, what mainly sets how much glycogen a muscle holds before a race?

options.text: How much carbohydrate per kg is eaten in the days before
options.why: Right: the authors conclude glycogen "primarily depends on quantity of CHO intake", with duration, training status and prior exercise also playing a part.

options.text: How much protein is eaten alongside the carbohydrate
options.why: The review named carbohydrate quantity, loading duration, training status and prior exercise as the effectors; protein was not among them.

options.text: Whether the athlete is a man or a woman
options.why: When women and men ate the same carbohydrate per kg, they stored the same amount of glycogen.

options.text: How many carbohydrate meals the day is split into
options.why: Meal frequency was not what the review identified; total carbohydrate per kg was.

variants.stem: A marathoner wants fuller muscle glycogen stores on race morning. Which change does the 2026 carbohydrate-loading meta-analysis point to first?

options.text: Eat more carbohydrate per kg in the last 36–48 h
options.why: Right: the quantity of carbohydrate was the main effector; the authors suggest over 8 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h.

options.text: Add a large protein shake to each meal
options.why: The review named carbohydrate quantity, not added protein, as the main lever.

options.text: Do a long hard run the evening before
options.why: Depleting exercise can speed loading when it comes 24–36 h ahead with enough carbohydrate; a hard run the night before mostly empties the store.

options.text: Spread the same food over more, smaller meals
options.why: The same total spread differently was not what the review found mattered; the total per kg was.

variants.stem: The carbohydrate-loading meta-analysis found that high intakes raised glycogen by 191.9 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass (95% CI 142.8 to 241.1), with I² = 94%. What does the I² tell you?

options.text: The trials disagree a lot on how big the rise is, so the best dose is uncertain
options.why: Right: I² near 94% means most of the spread between trials is real difference, not chance; the authors say this leaves the optimal intake uncertain.

options.text: There is a 94% chance that high carbohydrate raises glycogen
options.why: I² is not a probability that the effect is real; it describes how much the trial results differ beyond chance.

options.text: 94% of athletes respond to carbohydrate loading
options.why: I² is about differences between trials, not the share of people who respond.

options.text: The pooled effect is too small to matter in practice
options.why: The pooled rise is large and its interval is well above zero; I² speaks to consistency, not size.

variants.stem: A coach reads the 2026 carbohydrate-loading meta-analysis and concludes that over 8 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h will make his triathletes faster. What limits that conclusion most?

options.text: The outcome was muscle glycogen, not race performance
options.why: Right: the review measured glycogen from biopsies; faster racing is a further step the data don't test.

options.text: It pooled observational studies only, with no randomised trials
options.why: The meta-analysis kept 18 randomised trials with low risk of bias.

options.text: It was funded by a sports drink company
options.why: The authors declared no funding and no conflicts of interest.

options.text: It included no endurance-trained people
options.why: Many trials were in endurance-trained people; that group showed the clearest dose–response (r² = 0.490).

variants.stem: Which feature of the 2026 carbohydrate-loading meta-analysis most limits how far its dose advice applies to female runners?

options.text: Only 12% of participants were women, and cycle-phase effects are unclear
options.why: Right: only 74 of 641 participants were women, too few for a sex subgroup analysis, and the review found the effect of menstrual cycle phase on glycogen storage inconclusive.

options.text: Women stored much less glycogen than men at the same intake
options.why: The review found the opposite: at the same intake per kg, women stored the same as men.

options.text: Women were excluded from every trial in the review
options.why: Women were included in several trials; they were a minority, not absent.

options.text: Glycogen in women was measured only in the liver
options.why: All included trials measured muscle glycogen from biopsies, in women and men.
